clinicalPearls: Small-bowel injury from abdominal or pelvic radiotherapy, in acute and chronic forms
Acute enteritis causes nausea, cramping, diarrhoea and malabsorption during and shortly after treatment and usually settles
Chronic radiation enteropathy develops months to years later with obstruction, malabsorption, bleeding or fistulae
Fixed loops of small bowel in the pelvis (for example after surgery) are especially vulnerable
Chronic disease reflects progressive obliterative endarteritis, ischaemia and fibrosis
Management is largely supportive and nutritional; surgery for strictures or fistulae is high-risk in irradiated tissue
reference.pathophysiology: Radiation enteritis arises from ionising radiation injury to the rapidly dividing small-bowel mucosa and to the bowel vasculature. Acute injury causes mucosal cell loss, villous blunting and inflammation with malabsorption and diarrhoea, and usually recovers. Chronic radiation enteropathy results from progressive submucosal fibrosis and obliterative endarteritis, producing ischaemia, strictures, dysmotility, bacterial overgrowth, bleeding from telangiectasia and fistula formation. Risk relates to dose, technique and factors that fix bowel loops within the radiation field.
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging or contrast studies of the small bowel
Assessment of nutritional status and malabsorption
Endoscopy where accessible bowel is involved
Evaluation for bacterial overgrowth and bile acid malabsorption
redFlags: Severe malnutrition or features suggesting recurrent tumour
reference.prognosis: Acute enteritis usually resolves after treatment; chronic enteropathy is progressive and difficult to manage, with surgery carrying high complication rates in irradiated bowel.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic symptoms to recurrent cancer without considering radiation enteropathy (and vice versa)
Underestimating the surgical risk in irradiated bowel
Overlooking bacterial overgrowth and bile acid malabsorption as treatable contributors
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Supportive control of acute symptoms with antiemetics, antidiarrhoeal agents and rehydration during and shortly after radiotherapy
Nutritional support with a low-residue, low-fat diet, and parenteral nutrition where malabsorption is severe
Treatment of bile acid malabsorption with bile acid sequestrants and of small-bowel bacterial overgrowth with antibiotics
Endoscopic or surgical intervention reserved for strictures, obstruction or fistulae, recognising the high complication rate of operating on irradiated bowel
Long-term monitoring of nutritional status, weight and micronutrient and vitamin levels
Preventive optimisation of radiotherapy technique and dietitian-led multidisciplinary follow-up
